sections.heading: The idea
sections.figure_svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>state to transfer</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">C   (sI-A)^{-1}   B   +   D</text></svg>
sections.figure_alt: The formula G(s) = C(sI-A)^-1 B + D.
sections.body_md:
The transfer function of a state-space system summarizes the input-output behavior. The formula \(G(s) = C(sI - A)^{-1}B + D\) comes from taking the Laplace transform of the state equations and solving for the output.

The poles of \(G(s)\) are the values where \((sI - A)^{-1}\) blows up, which are the eigenvalues of \(A\). The zeros come from the numerator polynomial. A minimal realization has no pole-zero cancellations, so the transfer function order equals the state dimension.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
State equations:
\[
\dot{x} = Ax + Bu, \quad y = Cx + Du.
\]

Transfer function:
\[
G(s) = C(sI - A)^{-1}B + D.
\]

Poles: roots of \(\det(sI - A) = 0\) (eigenvalues of \(A\)).

DC gain: \(G(0) = -CA^{-1}B + D\) (assuming \(A\) invertible).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md: A first-order system has \(A = -3\), \(B = 2\), \(C = 4\), \(D = 0\). Then \((sI - A)^{-1} = 1/(s + 3)\). The transfer function is \(G(s) = 4 \cdot (1/(s+3)) \cdot 2 = 8/(s+3)\). The pole is at \(-3\), matching the eigenvalue. The DC gain is \(G(0) = 8/3 = 2.67\). Alternatively, \(-CA^{-1}B = -4 \cdot (-1/3) \cdot 2 = 8/3\).

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: The order matters: \(C\) on the left, \(B\) on the right. For MIMO systems, \(G\) is a matrix. Non-minimal realizations have hidden modes that cancel in the transfer function. The DC gain formula requires \(A\) to be invertible (no eigenvalue at zero).

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Realization goes the other way: from \(G(s)\) to state-space form, with non-uniqueness. Controllable and observable canonical forms are standard constructions. Balancing and reduction techniques trim states that contribute little to input-output behavior. Frequency response \(G(j\omega)\) is evaluated from either representation.
